At 8 weeks, kitty has become quite adept at climbing trees, and last night she caught and killed a mouse.

 
Especially with the morning sun, and after a cold night, she loves to dance and tangle with things for hours. Her dance is very animated and peculiar, with jumps, sidesteps, and arching back. 

She prefers to sleep in the warmth of my sleeping bag, but will not object to spending a night outside the tent. She has become attentive to the birds and various sounds of the desert. 

In the early morning hours, near the hotspring, which is just off the shoulder of Interstate 8, I see a lone full grown wild coyote. 

The hotspring is strategically located at the corner of a major wildlife quadrant. Once at the corner of this quadrant, wildlife might transition to the other 3 quadrants, but only through crossing a bridge spanning the All American Canal, or by going underneath two bridges of the Interstate highway. 

The two eastern quadrants are desert and sand dunes, whereas the two western quadrants are desert transformed into large scale agricultural farmland.  

Wildlife may visit the spring, but likely remain in their home quadrant, the northeast.  The hotspring conveniently marks the crossroads. Coyotes will remain and survive in the east, but likely be shot or run over in the west. 

I twice saw large black cat creatures on both the east and west sides, once a pack of four or five at the west of the canal bridge crossing. 

Kitty stays at the camp always, having never been to the hotspring. I have fashioned a basket an netting which I can strap down to the front rack of my bicycle. 

The morning after devouring her first mouse, I tested the basket with an 16 mile  round trip into Holtville. I let her free on the library lawn and she appears cautious and somewhat frightened at everything or anyone passing by.

She explores the new environment cautiously while remaining near, listening and looking attentively at everything.
